content: Freckles are clusters of concentrated melanin that are most commonly visible on individuals with fair complexions. A freckle is also referred to as an ephelis. The presence of freckles is determined by genetics and is associated with a specific variant of the melanocortin-1 receptor (MC1R) gene, which is a dominant trait. Freckles are frequently observed in individuals with fair hair, such as blonde, strawberry blonde, dishwater blonde, or most commonly, red hair. Ultraviolet B (UV-B) radiation activates melanocytes, the cells responsible for melanin production, leading to an increase in melanin synthesis. This process causes freckles to darken and become more numerous. Freckles are most commonly found on the face but can appear on any area of the skin that is exposed to sunlight. Freckles are rare in infants but are more commonly seen in children before puberty. They tend to be less prevalent in adults. However, in some cases, freckles may fade with age. It is important to note that freckles are not considered a skin disorder. Individuals with freckles typically have a lower concentration of photoprotective melanin, making them more vulnerable to the harmful effects of UV radiation. While there is ongoing debate regarding the safety of sunscreen, protective clothing is generally recommended as the preferred method of sun protection. There are two distinct types of freckles. The first type, known as ephelides, is a genetic trait. Ephelides are flat, light brown or red freckles that tend to fade during the winter months. They are more common in individuals with light skin tones. The regular use of sunblock can help suppress the appearance of ephelides. The second type of freckles includes liver spots, also referred to as sun spots or lentigines. Unlike ephelides, lentigines do not fade during the winter. Lentigines are more frequently observed in older individuals.
